plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the geometry of light refraction at a planar interface between two optical media, as described by Snell's law. A horizontal black line divides the scene into an upper region with refractive index n1 and a lower region with refractive index n2; a thick blue line traces the ray direction as it strikes the interface and continues into the second medium. A thin vertical line marks the surface normal at the point of incidence, with a small right-angle square confirming its perpendicularity to the interface; the angle theta_1 is measured between the incoming ray and the normal above the interface, and theta_2 is measured between the refracted ray and the normal below. The ray bends toward or away from the normal depending on the relative magnitudes of n1 and n2, embodying the relationship n1 sin theta_1 = n2 sin theta_2. This figure introduces refraction geometry as the physical basis for how lenses bend light and form images.

interactionPlan.concept: Snell's law relates the incident angle, refracted angle, and refractive indices at a boundary, explaining why light bends toward the normal, away from it, or undergoes total internal reflection.

interactions.label: Upper medium refractive index n₁
interactions.teaches: Increasing the refractive index of the incident medium makes total internal reflection possible when light tries to pass into a lower-index medium

interactions.teaches: Increasing the refractive index of the second medium bends the transmitted ray closer to the surface normal

demo_steps.title: Bending toward the normal
demo_steps.narration: With n₂ larger than n₁, the refracted ray enters a slower optical medium and bends closer to the surface normal. Drag the incident ray and watch θ₂ stay smaller than θ₁.

demo_steps.title: Bending away from the normal
demo_steps.narration: When n₁ is larger than n₂, the refracted ray bends away from the normal. The same incident angle now produces a larger θ₂.

demo_steps.title: Total internal reflection
demo_steps.narration: Keep n₁ greater than n₂ and drag θ₁ past the critical angle. The refracted ray disappears because Snell's law would require sin θ₂ to be greater than 1, so a reflected ray appears instead.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Light bends so that n sin θ stays matched across the boundary; if that match would require an impossible refracted angle, the light totally reflects instead.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean 2D SVG layout matching the textbook figure: a black horizontal interface across the center, upper region labeled n₁ and lower region labeled n₂ on the left, and a thin cyan vertical normal through the incidence point. Draw the incident and refracted rays as thick saturated blue segments meeting exactly at the interface. Angle labels θ₁ and θ₂ should sit near their respective arcs between each ray and the normal, not between the ray and the surface. Keep the right-angle marker at the normal-interface intersection. As the incident ray is dragged, rotate it about the incidence point and recompute the refracted ray from n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. When n₂ > n₁, the lower ray should visibly move closer to the normal; when n₁ > n₂, it should bend farther from the normal. If θ₁ exceeds the critical angle for n₁ > n₂, hide the refracted ray, show a symmetric reflected ray above the interface, and display a concise 'total internal reflection' annotation.
